svg.text: TCP Timer Management: The Four Core Timers
Forouzan Section 23.3 / RFC 6298 — Jacobson's RTO, Persistence Probe, Keepalive & 2MSL TIME-WAIT

g.text: 1. Retransmission Timer (RTO)
Purpose: Detect lost segments and trigger retransmission
• Dynamic calculation using Jacobson's Algorithm (RFC 6298):
SRTT = (1 - α)·SRTT + α·RTT (α = 1/8)
RTTVAR = (1 - β)·RTTVAR + β·|SRTT - RTT| (β = 1/4)
RTO = SRTT + 4 × RTTVAR (Min: 1.0s)
• Karn's Algorithm: Never measure RTT for retransmitted packets.
• Exponential Backoff: On timeout, double RTO (RTO = 2 × RTO).
2. Persistence Timer
Purpose: Prevent Zero-Window Deadlock
• Problem: Receiver advertises rwnd = 0. Later, receiver buffer frees up and sends rwnd = 2000, but this ACK is LOST!
• Result without timer: Deadlock! Sender waits for window update, receiver waits for incoming data forever.
• Action: Sender periodically transmits a 1-byte
Zero-Window Probe (ZWP) segment.
• Receiver responds with current rwnd, breaking the deadlock!
• Interval: Uses exponential backoff (typically 5s up to 60s).
3. Keepalive Timer
Purpose: Detect crashed or unreachable peer on idle line
• Prevents servers from holding resources for defunct clients.
• Default duration: Typically 2 hours of complete silence.
• Sends 9 probe segments, spaced 75 seconds apart.
• If no response after all probes: RST connection
and free server socket memory.
• Optional in base TCP; enabled via SO_KEEPALIVE socket option.
• Used widely in long-lived database connections and proxies.
4. TIME-WAIT (2MSL) Timer
Purpose: Graceful connection teardown & packet draining
• Runs on active-close endpoint after sending final ACK to FIN.
• Duration: 2 × Maximum Segment Lifetime (2MSL = 1 to 2 mins).
Reason 1: Ensure final ACK reached server.
If ACK lost, server resends FIN; client re-ACKs.
Reason 2: Drain lingering packets from network routes.
• Prevents duplicate packets of old connection from interfering with
a new connection on the same IP:Port socket pair.
